label: GPT-6.1 Sol
output:
Dear Kelechi,

You said if I was serious, I should put it in writing. So here we are. A proper letter, posted to your house in Croydon like we are waiting for the next ship to bring news from home. Please appreciate the effort. There was a stamp involved.

First, I want it recorded that you came to my birthday, ate my food and then gave me another instalment of *The Spreadsheet Is Killing Me*. Nine years at that firm, and apparently every day now looks like the day before, except somebody has changed a figure and you must discover which somebody. When I said you should come and teach maths, you laughed as if I had suggested you join the circus.

I was serious. I am still serious. But before you start composing your defence, I am not asking you to resign on Monday. I am asking you to come to an open evening with me. That is the whole request. You may finish this letter without becoming responsible for a single child.

We have known each other since Unilag, so I think I’m allowed to remind you of the person you were before costings became your whole personality. You were the one tutoring half our hostel in Moremi before exams. People would arrive convinced they knew nothing, and you would sit with them until something clicked. You never did that annoying thing clever people do where they explain the same thing again, only louder, then look offended when you still don’t understand.

You would try another way. Draw something. Find an example. Make a joke so the person could stop panicking. You made it possible to ask a stupid question without feeling stupid.

That is why I suggested teaching. Not just because you got an A in further maths, although I will happily bring that up whenever you pretend you don’t have the brains for it. Knowing maths matters, obviously. But being able to help somebody else understand it is a different thing, and I have watched you do that for years.

Look at Christmas. My nephew was fighting fractions as if they had personally insulted his mother. You got plates out and started dividing jollof into portions. By the end, he was explaining it back to you. He still talks about it. Meanwhile, some of us have actual teaching qualifications and were standing there holding drinks.

Please don’t let this enter your head. You are already difficult enough.

I’m telling you because I think you dismiss that side of yourself. To you, you were just helping a small boy with his homework. But you noticed what wasn’t working, found something he understood and stayed with him until he got there. You were patient. You were funny. You didn’t make him feel slow. Those things matter in a classroom.

Last month, a Year 11 boy I teach, Damola, finally got simultaneous equations after three weeks. Three weeks of us going back over it, trying different examples, getting somewhere and then apparently returning to our starting point. Then one day he looked at his working and shouted, “Is that all??”

As if I had spent three weeks hiding the easy version from him.

The whole class clapped. He was grinning, I was laughing, and for a minute everybody was just pleased for him. You would have loved it.

That doesn’t happen every lesson. Some lessons, the thing you carefully planned falls flat and somebody is asking for a pen you watched them put in their pocket thirty seconds ago. But when a child who has decided they cannot do maths discovers that they can, it stays with you. You go home knowing something happened that day.

Now, because you know me, and because you will rightly distrust a letter that makes teaching sound like one long inspirational film, let me tell you the other side.

Teaching is hard. The marking is endless. You finish one pile and another one appears, as if the books are reproducing in your bag. Behaviour some days is serious wahala. You can spend ages preparing something and still have a lesson where you feel you have achieved almost nothing. There is noise, there are demands, there are days when your patience has finished but you still have two lessons left.

When I started in 2019, I cried in the car park twice in my first term. Twice that I am admitting to in a document you can keep.

I don’t want you coming back to me in October saying, “But you said the children would love me.” I think they would. That will not stop them testing you. Being patient and funny gives you something useful to build on; it doesn’t mean you walk in already knowing how to run a classroom. You would have to learn. You would make mistakes. Some days you would wonder why you left a job where, whatever else was wrong, a spreadsheet never shouted across the room.

It does get better. You learn what to do, and you stop treating every difficult lesson as proof that you are useless. You find people who will help you. You get to know the children properly, including the ones who initially seem determined to shorten your life. But I won’t pretend the hard parts disappear.

And yes, there would be a pay drop in the first year. I know you have bills. I have not forgotten that adulthood is expensive just because I have found a use for coloured whiteboard pens.

The route I’m talking about is the salaried one: you get paid while you train, it takes one year, and the start would be September 2027. That makes it worth investigating, not automatically affordable. You would need to ask exactly what the salary is, look at your outgoings and see whether it works. There’s the pension to consider, the holidays, and pay progression afterwards. The holidays are a real benefit, even though schoolwork has an irritating habit of coming home with you. None of that means you should wave away the first-year drop. Get the figures. You, of all people, should enjoy that part.

Also, you are 34. Please stop behaving as if changing direction requires permission from your grandchildren. A woman in my department started at 41. Your nine years as a quantity surveyor would not vanish because you entered a classroom. You would be bringing experience of working with people, deadlines and actual uses for numbers. And you would still have things to learn, which might be good for you, Mr Same Spreadsheet Every Day.

At our school in Peckham, we have about 1,100 children. Two of our Year 9 maths groups have had a supply teacher covering them since September. I mention that because the need for maths teachers is very real to me. It has faces and exercise books attached to it.

But I’m not asking you to change careers out of guilt, or to come and rescue my timetable. That would be a terrible basis for a decision. I’m asking because I think there is a chance you would be good at this, and a chance it would give you something you are missing now.

On your last birthday, you said, “I just want to do something that matters before 40.”

I remember because you weren’t joking when you said it. I’m not saying your current work doesn’t matter. Somebody needs to check those costings, and I would prefer buildings not to be financed on vibes. But I do wonder whether the job is using enough of you. I hear you talk about work, then I watch you help somebody understand something, and you seem much more yourself doing the second thing.

That is worth an evening, surely.

So here are the details, written properly so you cannot claim I only mentioned it in passing:

**Thursday 19 November 2026, at 6pm. The open evening at the training partnership in Lewisham.**

I can go with you. Applications for next September open soon, so this is a good time to find out what is involved. Ask about the salary, the workload, the training and the support. Ask the awkward questions. You have been professionally questioning other people’s figures for nine years; don’t become shy now.

You do not have to sign anything. You do not have to announce a career change. We can go, listen and talk afterwards. If you come away thinking it isn’t for you, fair enough. At least you will know a bit more than you did when you laughed at me over birthday food.

But if part of you is interested, abeg, give that part a hearing before you talk yourself out of it.

Text me when this arrives. First, because I need to know whether posting letters still works. Second, to tell me you’re coming.

Your friend since Unilag,  
the one who has apparently become your careers adviser without payment
